subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 16. In this unit you will learn to interpret results – to take data that has already been collected and displayed, and work out what it actually means. This is one of the most useful skills in the whole of mathematics, because we live in a world flooded with numbers. Every day you meet data in news reports, on social media, in adverts, in weather forecasts, in football league tables and in the prices at the Hargeisa market. The people who can read that data carefully, and spot when it is being used to mislead them, are the people who make good decisions.

outcomes: Read and interpret bar charts, line graphs, pie charts and frequency tables, and know which display suits which kind of data.
Calculate the mean, median, mode and range of a data set and explain what each one tells you.
Choose the most appropriate average for a given situation and justify your choice.

Describe trends, patterns and outliers in data, and interpret what they mean in context.
Distinguish between correlation and causation and avoid the classic trap of confusing them.
Judge whether a sample is fair and identify common types of bias.
Recognise misleading graphs and statistical claims, and explain why they mislead.

concepts.title: Types of Data and Ways to Show It
concepts.explanation:
Before you can interpret results, you must know what kind of data you are looking at, because the kind of data decides which display and which calculations make sense. Data falls into two big families. Categorical data describes qualities that fall into named groups – favourite fruit, type of transport, or which football team someone supports. You cannot find the average of categories; there is no such thing as an ‘average favourite fruit’. Numerical data consists of measurements or counts – heights, temperatures, the number of goats in a herd – and you *can* do arithmetic with it, finding means and ranges.

Numerical data splits further. Discrete data can only take separate, countable values, like the number of children in a family (you cannot have 2.5 children). Continuous data can take any value in a range, like height or the mass of a sack of rice, because between any two values there is always another. Knowing which type you have keeps you from choosing a silly display.

Here is a quick guide to the four displays you will meet most often in this unit:

Bar chart – best for categorical data. The height of each bar shows the frequency of each group. Bars have gaps between them.

Line graph – best for showing how something changes over time, such as temperature through a day or a shop’s sales over a year.

Pie chart – best for showing how a whole is divided into parts, such as how a family spends its monthly income.

Frequency table – a tidy way to organise raw data into groups before you draw a chart or calculate an average.
concepts.example: Let us read a real display. Suppose a bar chart shows the favourite fruit of 30 pupils at Nuur Academy: mango 12, banana 9, papaya 6, dates 3. Straight away you can interpret it. The mode – the most popular fruit – is mango, because its bar is tallest. Twelve out of thirty pupils, which is nearly half, chose mango. Dates were least popular. Notice what the chart cannot tell you: it says nothing about *why* mango is popular, or whether pupils at another school would answer the same way. Reading a chart means stating clearly both what it shows and what it does not.

concepts.title: The Mean, Median and Mode
concepts.explanation:
When we describe a set of numbers, we often want a single value that stands for the whole set – a typical value, or average. In everyday speech people say ‘average’ as if there is only one, but in mathematics there are three different averages, and each has its own strengths. Choosing the right one is a real skill.

The mean is what most people picture. You add up all the values and divide by how many there are. Suppose Amina records how many goats five families own: 8, 12, 10, 6, 14. The total is 8 + 12 + 10 + 6 + 14 = 50, and there are 5 families, so the mean is 50 ÷ 5 = 10 goats. The mean uses every value, which is its great strength, but that is also its weakness: a single very large or very small value can drag it far from the centre.

The median is the middle value when the data is placed in order. Put the goat counts in order: 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. The value in the middle is 10. When there is an even number of values there is no single middle, so you take the mean of the two middle values. For 6, 8, 10, 12 the two middle numbers are 8 and 10, and their mean is (8 + 10) ÷ 2 = 9. The median’s great strength is that extreme values barely affect it.

The mode is the value that appears most often. In the set 4, 7, 7, 7, 9, 11 the mode is 7. A set can have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode at all if every value appears just once. The mode is the only average that works for categorical data – it is the only sensible way to describe an ‘average’ favourite fruit.
concepts.example: Why keep three averages instead of one? Because they can tell different stories. Imagine the monthly wages, in thousands of shillings, of five workers in a small workshop: 15, 16, 16, 17, 96. The last worker is the owner. The mean is (15 + 16 + 16 + 17 + 96) ÷ 5 = 160 ÷ 5 = 32, yet not one ordinary worker earns anywhere near 32 – the single huge value has pulled the mean up. The median is the middle value, 16, which describes a typical worker far more honestly. This is exactly why news reports about income usually use the median: it resists being dragged around by a few very large values.

concepts.title: The Range and the Spread of Data
concepts.explanation:
An average tells you where the middle of the data sits, but it says nothing about how spread out the values are. Two data sets can share the same mean yet look completely different. Consider the test marks of two pupils out of 10 across five tests. Hassan scores 6, 6, 7, 6, 5 and Yusuf scores 1, 10, 2, 9, 8. Both have a total of 30 and so a mean of 6, but Hassan is steady and reliable while Yusuf is wildly up and down. The average alone hides this. To describe spread, we need another number.

The simplest measure of spread is the range: the highest value minus the lowest value. For Hassan the range is 7 − 5 = 2, a small spread showing consistency. For Yusuf the range is 10 − 1 = 9, a large spread showing that his marks jump about. Now the two pupils are properly described: same average, very different consistency. A small range means the data is consistent; a large range means it is variable.

The range is quick and easy, but it has one weakness you must always keep in mind: it uses only the two most extreme values, so a single unusual value can make it misleading. If Yusuf had scored 1, 6, 6, 6, 6 his range would still be a large-looking 5 even though four of his marks are identical. Because of this, statisticians often prefer a measure that looks at the middle of the data – the interquartile range, which you will meet next.
concepts.example: Whenever you compare two groups, get into the habit of quoting an average and a measure of spread together. ‘The two classes had the same mean mark, but Class A had a much smaller range, so its results were more consistent.’ That single sentence is proper statistical interpretation: it captures both the typical value and how tightly the data clusters around it.

concepts.title: Quartiles and the Interquartile Range
concepts.explanation:
To describe spread more fairly, we split ordered data into four equal parts using quartiles. Imagine lining up all the values from smallest to largest. The median cuts the line in half. The lower quartile (Q1) sits a quarter of the way along, and the upper quartile (Q3) sits three-quarters of the way along. One quarter of the data lies below Q1, and one quarter lies above Q3.

The interquartile range (IQR) is Q3 − Q1. It measures the spread of the middle half of the data, which is why it is so useful: it ignores the extreme few values at each end and focuses on where most of the data actually lives. A small IQR means the middle of the data is tightly packed; a large IQR means it is widely spread.
concepts.example: Let us work one carefully. Here are the number of press-ups nine pupils could do: 5, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 18, 40. There are 9 values, already in order. The median is the 5th value, 12. The lower half is 5, 8, 9, 11, whose median (the mean of 8 and 9) is Q1 = 8.5. The upper half is 14, 15, 18, 40, whose median (the mean of 15 and 18) is Q3 = 16.5. So the IQR = 16.5 − 8.5 = 8. Notice that the value 40 is a clear outlier, yet it barely affects the IQR, whereas it would badly distort the ordinary range (40 − 5 = 35). This is the IQR’s great advantage.

concepts.title: Trends, Patterns and Outliers
concepts.explanation:
Once data is displayed, one of your main jobs is to describe its overall shape rather than getting lost in single points. On a line graph, look first for the trend – the general direction of travel. An upward trend shows something growing, a downward trend shows decline, and a flat trend shows little change. When Farah plots the monthly rainfall in Mogadishu and sees the line climbing from March to May, she can report an upward trend even though one or two months dipped slightly.

Beyond the overall trend, look for patterns. Many things repeat in cycles: market takings rise every Friday, temperatures rise and fall with the seasons, and a shop is busiest at particular hours. A repeating up-and-down pattern is called a seasonal or cyclical pattern. Spotting it helps people plan – a trader who knows sales peak before Eid can stock up in good time.
concepts.example: A word of caution about trends: never assume a trend will simply continue. If a plant’s height has doubled every week for three weeks, it will not keep doubling forever – it would soon be taller than a house. Extending a line beyond the data you actually have is called extrapolation, and it must always be done cautiously, because the pattern that held in the past may not hold in the future.

concepts.title: Correlation and Causation
concepts.explanation:
When we plot two things against each other, we often find a correlation – a relationship where they tend to change together. In positive correlation, as one goes up the other tends to go up too; taller people tend to have larger shoe sizes. In negative correlation, as one goes up the other tends to go down; the more time a phone spends switched on, the lower its battery. Some pairs show no correlation at all; a person’s shoe size has nothing to do with their favourite colour.

Here is the single most important idea in the whole unit, so read it twice: correlation does not prove causation. Just because two things rise and fall together does not mean one *causes* the other. Every year, ice-cream sales and the number of people swimming both rise at the same time. They are strongly correlated, but ice cream does not cause swimming, and swimming does not cause ice-cream sales. A third factor – hot weather – causes both. This hidden third factor is why so many statistical arguments go wrong.
concepts.example: Consider a real-sounding claim: “Pupils who own more books get higher marks, so buying books makes you cleverer.” The correlation may well be real, but the conclusion is a trap. Families who own many books often also have quiet study space, educated parents and time to read together – any of these could be the true cause. To show that one thing genuinely causes another, you need more than a correlation; you need a carefully controlled comparison. Whenever someone jumps from ‘these two things are linked’ to ‘so this one causes that one’, your alarm should ring.

methods.title: How to find the median
methods.example: Seven families own these numbers of goats: 12, 9, 15, 9, 20, 11, 9. Find the mean, median, mode and range.
steps: Put all the values in order from smallest to largest.
If there is an odd number of values, the median is the single middle one.
If there is an even number, the median is the mean of the two middle values.

methods.title: How to find the interquartile range
methods.example: A shop’s daily sales for a week are 40, 42, 41, 43, 40, 42 and 200 (the last was a special festival day). Which average best describes a typical day, and why?
steps: Put the data in order and find the median.
Find Q1, the median of the lower half of the data.
Find Q3, the median of the upper half of the data.
Subtract: IQR = Q3 − Q1.

methods.title: How to check whether a graph is misleading
methods.example: Two classes sit the same test out of 20. Class A scores have mean 14 and range 4. Class B scores have mean 14 and range 15. Compare the two classes.
steps: Check whether the vertical axis starts at zero.
Check that the scale is even and every axis is clearly labelled.
Ask what data might be missing or hidden.
Ask who made the graph and what they want you to believe.

methods.title: Interquartile range
methods.example: Find the median, quartiles and interquartile range of: 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15.
steps: There are 8 values, already in order.
The two middle values are 9 and 10, so the median = (9 + 10) ÷ 2 = 9.5.
The lower half is 4, 6, 7, 9, whose middle pair is 6 and 7, giving Q1 = 6.5.
The upper half is 10, 12, 13, 15, whose middle pair is 12 and 13, giving Q3 = 12.5.

methods.title: Correlation and causation
methods.example: A report finds that villages with more mobile phones also have higher exam results, and concludes that giving pupils phones raises exam results. What is wrong with this conclusion?
steps: The report has confused correlation with causation.
The two things rise together, but that does not prove one causes the other.
A hidden third factor — such as villages being wealthier, with better schools, more electricity and more educated parents — could cause both the higher phone ownership and the higher results.
To claim that phones *cause* better results you would need a controlled comparison, not just a correlation.

methods.title: Spot the misleading graph
methods.example: A bar chart of a shop’s profit shows two bars, one clearly twice as tall as the other, and the headline reads ‘Profit doubles!’. On closer look, the vertical axis runs from 90 to 100, and the bars represent 94 and 98. Is the headline fair?
steps: No.
Because the axis starts at 90 instead of 0, a small rise from 94 to 98 — an increase of just 4 units, or about 4% — is stretched to look like a doubling.
If the axis started at zero, the two bars would look almost the same height.
The graph is misleading; profit rose only slightly, not by anything like double.

workedExamples.title: Find the mean, median, mode and range
workedExamples.prompt: Seven families own these numbers of goats: 12, 9, 15, 9, 20, 11, 9. Find the mean, median, mode and range.
workedExamples.solution: Total = 12 + 9 + 15 + 9 + 20 + 11 + 9 = 85. There are 7 values, so the mean = 85 ÷ 7 = 12.1 (to 1 decimal place). Put them in order: 9, 9, 9, 11, 12, 15, 20. The middle (4th) value is the median = 11. The value 9 appears most often, so the mode = 9. The range = 20 − 9 = 11.

workedExamples.title: Choose the best average
workedExamples.prompt: A shop’s daily sales for a week are 40, 42, 41, 43, 40, 42 and 200 (the last was a special festival day). Which average best describes a typical day, and why?
workedExamples.solution: The mean = (40+42+41+43+40+42+200) ÷ 7 = 448 ÷ 7 = 64, but no ordinary day is anywhere near 64 — the festival day of 200 is an outlier that has dragged the mean up. Ordered: 40, 40, 41, 42, 42, 43, 200, so the median = 42, which describes a typical day honestly. The median is the better average here because it resists the outlier.

workedExamples.title: Compare two data sets
workedExamples.prompt: Two classes sit the same test out of 20. Class A scores have mean 14 and range 4. Class B scores have mean 14 and range 15. Compare the two classes.
workedExamples.solution: Both classes have the same mean of 14, so on average they performed equally well. But Class A has a much smaller range (4), meaning its marks are consistent and clustered together, while Class B has a large range (15), meaning its marks are very spread out — some pupils did very well and others struggled. So although the averages match, Class A is far more consistent, and Class B contains both stronger and weaker pupils.

workedExamples.title: Interquartile range
workedExamples.prompt: Find the median, quartiles and interquartile range of: 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15.
workedExamples.solution: There are 8 values, already in order. The two middle values are 9 and 10, so the median = (9 + 10) ÷ 2 = 9.5. The lower half is 4, 6, 7, 9, whose middle pair is 6 and 7, giving Q1 = 6.5. The upper half is 10, 12, 13, 15, whose middle pair is 12 and 13, giving Q3 = 12.5. The IQR = 12.5 − 6.5 = 6.

workedExamples.title: Judge a sample
workedExamples.prompt: Sahra wants to know the favourite subject of all 500 pupils in her school. She asks 15 pupils in the library after school. Explain two problems with her method and suggest a better one.
workedExamples.solution: First, the sample is too small — 15 out of 500 is unlikely to reflect everyone. Second, pupils in the library after school are not representative: they are probably keen readers, so subjects like reading may be over-chosen (selection bias). A better method is random sampling: number all 500 pupils and use a random list to pick, say, 50 of them, so every pupil has an equal chance and the sample fairly reflects the whole school.

workedExamples.title: Find a missing value from the mean
workedExamples.prompt: Four pupils have a mean height of 150 cm. Three of them are 148 cm, 152 cm and 149 cm. How tall is the fourth pupil?
workedExamples.solution: If the mean of 4 values is 150, the total must be 4 × 150 = 600 cm. The three known heights add to 148 + 152 + 149 = 449 cm. So the fourth pupil is 600 − 449 = 151 cm. Working backwards from the mean to a total is a powerful trick worth remembering.

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: Two classes take a spelling test. Class A: mean 8, range 3. Class B: mean 8, range 9. Write one sentence comparing them.
workedExamples.solution: Both classes averaged 8, but Class A (range 3) was far more consistent than Class B (range 9).

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: Describe the type of correlation you would expect between: a) hours of study and test score b) outdoor temperature and hot-drink sales.
workedExamples.solution: a) Hours of study and test score — positive correlation, since more study tends to mean a higher score. b) Outdoor temperature and hot-drink sales — negative correlation, since hotter weather tends to mean fewer hot drinks sold.

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: A pie chart shows how Hani’s family spends its monthly income: food 40%, rent 25%, transport 15%, savings 10%, other 10%. On what does the family spend the most, and what fraction goes on rent?
workedExamples.solution: The family spends the most on food (40%). Rent is 25%, which is 25/100 = 1/4 (one quarter) of their income.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: Six numbers have a mean of 15. Five of them are 12, 18, 14, 16 and 11. Find the sixth number.
workedExamples.solution: Total = 6 × 15 = 90; five known add to 71; sixth number = 90 − 71 = 19.

activities.title: Household Data Hunt
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and things around your home to count or measure.
steps: Choose something you can collect ten values of – shoe sizes of family members, the mass of ten mangoes, or the number of pages in ten books.
Write your data in a list, then put it in order.

rules.title: Finding the Mean, Median, Mode and Range
rules.text: Mean = the total of all the values divided by how many values there are. Median = put the data in order; if there is an odd number of values, take the single middle one, and if there is an even number, take the mean of the two middle values. Mode = the value that occurs most often (a data set can have no mode, one mode, or more than one). Range = the highest value minus the lowest value.

rules.title: Finding the Quartiles and the Interquartile Range
rules.text: Put the data in order and find the median, which splits it in half. The lower quartile (Q1) is the median of the lower half of the data, and the upper quartile (Q3) is the median of the upper half. The interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 − Q1, and it describes the spread of the middle half of the data without being affected by extreme outliers.

rules.title: Judging Correlation, Causation and Misleading Graphs
rules.text: A correlation is positive if both values tend to rise together, negative if one rises as the other falls, and zero if there is no clear link. Correlation alone never proves causation – always ask whether a hidden third factor could explain both things changing together. Before trusting a graph, check that the vertical axis starts at zero, the scale is even, and nothing important has been left out; before trusting a sample, check that it is large enough and chosen fairly, not just from one group of people.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Trends, Patterns and Outliers.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A trend is the general direction data moves in over time — upward, downward, or flat. A pattern may be a repeating cycle, such as sales rising every weekend. reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Correlation and Causation.
